newsitem.title: FRANCE: French envoy seeks ties with Kabila. [CORRECTED 19:35 GMT]
newsitem.headline: French envoy seeks ties with Kabila. [CORRECTED 19:35 GMT]

text.p: A French envoy just back from a mission to Kinshasa to initiate ties with newly installed President Laurent Kabila said on Thursday he was told the existing poor relations with Paris stemmed from a lack of communications.
The envoy, senior diplomat Jean-Pierre Lafon, told reporters he was not received by Kabili as the British and American ambassadors there had been.

France was long the main foreign backer of fallen president Mobutu Sese Seko. Paris had actively opposed Kabila, who was seen bysome French officials as a "puppet" of English-speaking East African states manipulated by Washington in a bid to end French influence in the region.

"The foreign minister of the Democratic Republic of Congo (Bizima Karaha) told me that misunderstandings with France were a result of a lack of communications," Lafon said. (Corrects name of foreign minister)
He said he told the minister Paris was attached to democracy, human rights, protection of refugees, Congolese unity and increased French investment in the country.
Lafon added that France's ambassador to Kinshasa expected to meet Kabila soon and authorities of the new government said they wanted French nationals established in the former Zaire to remain.
Lafon's visit was sparked by the killing of two French citizens by uniformed men in Kinshasa soon after Kabila's forces overthrew Mobutu this month.

French troops in the Congo Republic, just across the Congo river separating the two states, where meanwhile helping its small army round up refugees from former Zaire to avoid instability across its borders, French defence officials said.

"About 15,000 refugees have crossed the river into the Congo from the former Zaire and our troops have been placed at the disposal of the Congo army and the NGOs (non-government organisations) to face up to the situation," Defence Ministry spokesman Pierre Servent told reporters in Paris.
A senior military aide explained that "the Congo army does not have the means to go and control, re-group and eventually disarm those who crossed over with weapons".
The aim of the local government and of the aid groups was to concentrate refugees in two camps away from Brazzaville, the officer said.

The French troops, initially sent to the Congo capital Brazzavile to be ready to cross over to Kinshasa to protect foreign nationals if needed, would give logistical help to the Congo army, primarily moving its forces around by aircraft or lorry, he said.
There are about 400 French troops in Brazzaville, mostly Foreign Legion paratroopers.

"The Congo government has made clear it does not want these refugees to stay in the Congo. The past experiences of Zaire have served as a lesson to other African countries," said the aide, referring to the spillover of the Rwanda crisis into Zaire, ultimately leading to the downfall of President Mobutu Sese Seko.
The aide recalled that a presidential election was scheduled in the Congo on July 27 and its govermment wished to avoid anything that could trouble law and order.
The Paris-based press defence group Reporters Without Borders (RSF) accused Kabila, of continuing past methods of intimidating both the local and the foreign press covering his country.
